question: How does a single melodic line mark a phrase ending without a chord?
intro: A single voice carries the melody without a harmonic accompaniment. Listen for the recurring shape of the chant as successive stanzas give it new words.

sections.label: Opening stanzas
sections.mNote: one melodic line; the hymn’s recurring stanza tune

sections.label: Continuing stanzas
sections.mNote: the same tune carries further Latin text

sections.label: Later stanzas
sections.mNote: strophic continuation, leading to the final sustained close

cues.title: A melody without chords
cues.text: Gareth Hughes sings alone. Follow the rise and fall of the line and the spaces between phrases: in monophony, a single melody supplies the shape without a separate bass or chordal accompaniment.
cues.evidence: The Commons description identifies Hughes and the traditional mode-III plainchant. This concerns the recording’s solo texture, not an onset measured at zero. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pange_Lingua_Latin_in_Latin.ogg

cues.title: Aquinas supplies the text
cues.text: Thomas Aquinas wrote this Eucharistic hymn for the Office of Corpus Christi in the thirteenth century. That authorship belongs to the words; it does not establish that Aquinas composed the traditional melody heard here.
cues.evidence: Hugh Henry, Catholic Encyclopedia, “The Hymn of St. Thomas Aquinas”, identifies the author, century and liturgical function. The recording source calls the melody traditional. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/11441c.htm

cues.title: The stanza tune returns
cues.text: Throughout the hymn, compare successive phrases with the tune already heard. New syllables alter the delivery while the recurring melodic outline holds the stanzas together; recurrence matters more than a succession of new themes.
cues.evidence: The six-stanza hymn is strophic. The report’s low-level windows around 0:30, 1:00 and 1:35 support broad phrase groupings, not word alignment or exact stanza starts. The section markers group the continuing hymn approximately.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Two hymns share an opening
cues.text: Aquinas’s hymn is not the older Passion hymn beginning with the same words, usually credited to Venantius Fortunatus. Aquinas takes up its verse pattern but writes a different text about the Eucharist.
cues.evidence: The Catholic Encyclopedia distinguishes the Passion and Blessed Sacrament hymns and describes Aquinas’s imitation of the earlier metre. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/11441c.htm

cues.title: A shorter separate hymn
cues.text: The last two stanzas also circulate as Tantum ergo, sung at Benediction. This file preserves the longer Pange lingua recording rather than the separately cropped two-stanza derivative on Commons.
cues.evidence: The Catholic Encyclopedia explains the separate Tantum ergo use; Commons links its cropped derivative. This is contextual information, not a claim that the words Tantum ergo begin at 2:16.

cues.title: The final rise and release
cues.text: The late part of this performance reaches a stronger recorded crest before the line subsides. Follow the last sustained sound into its release rather than expecting an instrumental chord to finish the hymn.
cues.evidence: The report places the loudest five-second window at 2:50, then declining level and onset density across 3:15–3:25. It does not establish a particular vowel, pitch or breath at this cue.

transitions.title: The stanza melody carries the next text
transitions.how: The hymn continues by returning to its stanza tune, not by changing ensemble or introducing a contrasting theme. With only one voice, the end of a phrase and the renewed melodic contour do the work that a chordal cadence might do in accompanied music. The marker groups the continuing stanzas; it does not identify an exact syllable or breath.
transitions.evidence: The documented six-stanza hymn supplies the strophic design. The measured level trough near 1:00 and renewed level around 1:05–1:10 support an approximate grouping here. No word-level or stanza-number alignment has been made.

transitions.title: The same melody continues towards the close
transitions.how: Further stanzas keep the same monophonic plan. The new words fit the established melodic phrases, while brief gaps separate their delivery. Continuity comes from the returning tune rather than a harmonic modulation or a new instrumental colour; this broad marker does not locate the opening of Tantum ergo.
transitions.evidence: The report shows a level trough near 2:05 followed by a renewed rise at 2:10–2:15, consistent with the hymn’s recurring phrase groups. The timing remains approximate; no sung word is assigned to 2:09.
